metaTitle: Best Long Reach Cordless Pole Hedge Trimmers
metaDescription: Six long reach cordless pole hedge trimmers compared on real pole length versus claimed reach, head control, weight and battery, so tall hedges stay safe.
expertTake: The Alloyman 16 inch with two 4.0Ah packs is the best long-reach pick for honest pole length and runtime, and the YDlawn 22 inch is the pick for reach with a wide blade. The Craftsman tool-only model is the choice for V20 owners. If a hedge needs more than about 12 feet of real reach, hire a pro or use a ladder with a handheld.
introParagraphs: Long reach is the main sales claim of a pole trimmer, and it is also the most misleading one. A headline figure usually adds your own height to the pole, so the real height you can cut is lower than the number on the box.

What decides whether a long reach is usable is control at full extension: shaft stiffness, head angles and weight at the tip. This guide ranks six models by how much honest reach they give and how well they behave when stretched.

products.name: Alloyman 20V MAX 16 in. Telescoping Pole Hedge Trimmer, Two 4.0Ah Batteries

specList.label: Pole
specList.value: Telescopic, up to 8 ft, folds shorter

products.description:
This is the honest long-reach tool. The telescopic pole is listed at up to 8 feet when unfolded, which is a pole length and not a vague reach claim, and it folds up short for storage. The 16 inch hardened steel dual-action blades cut to 3/4 inch at 1,400 strokes per minute, which is above the capacity of most 16 inch pole heads.

It weighs 8 pounds, which is heavy for a pole tool, and that weight sits in the shaft and the two packs. The non-slip rubber grip helps, but there is no strap, so you rely on technique. A short blade keeps the tip load down at full extension, and two 4.0Ah packs give you enough runtime to finish a long hedge in two stints.

In practice, a user of average height gets a working height of around 11 to 12 feet from this pole. That is enough for most garden hedges. Keep the telescopic joint clean and the clamp tight, wipe the blades after use and store the packs indoors. Next to the YDlawn, it trades blade width for capacity and a stiffer feel. Test the pole at the length you actually plan to use before you start a long session, since a joint that creeps under load is easier to notice at ground level than at full stretch.
products.bestFor: Tall hedges where honest reach and runtime both matter.
pros: 8 ft telescopic pole with honest length
3/4 in. capacity on a 16 inch blade
cons: 8 lb is tiring at full extension

products.name: YDlawn 20V 22 in. Cordless Pole Hedge Trimmer, 15 ft Claimed Reach, 2 x 4.0Ah
products.description:
YDlawn's headline is 15 feet of reach, but the specification that matters is the 8 foot telescopic pole beneath it. The 15 feet is the pole length plus the user's own height with arms raised, so the standing reach on a hedge top is nearer 12 to 13 feet. That is still very good, and it is the highest real reach in this lineup.

The 22 inch dual-action blade is the widest here, and it is cut to 5/8 inch, a smaller capacity than the Alloyman's 3/4 inch. That is the tradeoff: a wide blade covers a long flat top in fewer passes, but it bogs down on woody stems earlier. The listing quotes up to 2 hours of runtime across two 4.0Ah packs and a fast charger.

A 22 inch head at the end of a long pole is a lot of leverage, so the tool tires you faster than the 16 inch Alloyman at the same reach. Keep the head angle shallow and let the pole rest on your hip when you can. Clean the blades after every session and store the shaft collapsed. If you have a long flat top that is only lightly overgrown, this is where the wide head pays off, because you can sweep a full body-length in one pass. On thicker growth, switch to the Alloyman for its higher capacity.
products.bestFor: Long, flat, softly grown hedge tops at height.
pros: Highest real reach in this lineup
22 inch blade is the widest here
Two 4.0Ah packs and a fast charger
cons: 5/8 in. capacity is below the Alloyman
Wide blade adds leverage at full extension

products.name: Craftsman CMCPHT818B V20 18 in. Cordless Pole Hedge Trimmer, Tool Only
products.description:
Craftsman's bare pole trimmer is the long-reach tool for people who already own V20 batteries. The listing gives up to 11 feet of reach, a figure that includes your own height like most pole-tool claims, and an 18 inch dual-action blade that cuts to 3/4 inch. A 180 degree pivoting head locks into five positions.

The head design is the same as on the brand's kit version, so the difference is the missing battery and charger. That makes it cheaper only if you own V20 packs. A smaller reach than the YDlawn's claim is balanced by a heavier-duty capacity and a more established parts network.

A shaft this long flexes under load, so keep the head angle near 30 to 45 degrees and do not extend more than you need. Store it collapsed, wipe the blades after use and keep the pack indoors. If you do not own V20, one of the complete kits in this guide will cost less to start. For a tall hedge, the ability to reach the top with the shaft partly collapsed is a safer approach than full stretch, so plan to stand a little further back. V20 spare packs are common, which eases the runtime question.
products.bestFor: Craftsman V20 owners who need a tall-hedge tool.
pros: 3/4 in. capacity with an 18 inch blade

products.name: Xssive 20V Cordless Telescopic Pole Hedge Trimmer, Shoulder Strap, 3 kg
products.description:
Xssive builds this pole trimmer around comfort at height. The listed weight of 3 kilograms, about 6.6 pounds, is lighter than most telescopic poles, and a D-shaped auxiliary handle and shoulder strap spread the load across your body. A pivoting head locks in place for precise horizontal and vertical cuts.

The motor runs at 1,400 RPM no-load, which is typical for the class. The kit includes one 2.0Ah battery, which is the weakest pack in this guide, so expect short sessions or buy a spare. The listing does not give a blade capacity figure, so treat it as a light-duty tool.

The strap is the point. On a long pole, the way you carry the weight matters more than the weight itself, and this design suits anyone whose wrists tire first. Inspect the strap clips each season and wipe the blades after each use. Pair it with a second battery if you plan to hedge anything longer than a short boundary. A strap also makes it easier to rest the tool mid-job without having to set it down on the ground.
products.bestFor: Users who tire from holding a pole and cut light growth.
pros: 3 kg is lighter than most telescopic poles
Shoulder strap and D-handle share the load

products.name: 20V 18 in. Cordless Pole Hedge Trimmer, 6 lb, Two 2000mAh Batteries, 6.3 to 8.6 ft
products.description:
This kit sits between the heavy Alloyman and the strap-based Xssive. At 6 pounds it is light for an 18 inch pole head, and the telescopic pole adjusts from 6.3 to 8.6 feet, so you can set the length to the job rather than carry full extension all the time. Two 2000mAh batteries are included, with a listed 60 minute runtime on both.

The 1,400 RPM motor is the same speed as others in the class, and the 18 inch dual-action blade is a good compromise on tip weight. The seller is not a major brand, so parts and warranty support are thin and you should read the return terms before buying.

It makes sense for hedges that are tall but not thick, when keeping the tool light matters more than power. Collapse the pole after use, wipe the blades and keep the packs indoors. Compared with the Alloyman at 8 pounds it is easier to hold, but its packs are half the size. If you only cut on dry, mild days, the smaller packs are less of a handicap, since cold is what truly drains them. It is a reasonable second pole tool for family members who find 8 pounds too much.
products.bestFor: Tall, lightly grown hedges and users who prefer a lighter tool.
pros: 6 lb is light for an 18 inch pole head

products.name: MZK 20V 23 in. Cordless Hedge Trimmer with Extension Pole, 2 x 4Ah, 0 to 120 Degrees
products.description:
MZK offers a 22.4 inch handheld trimmer that takes an extension pole, and a head that moves through five positions across 0 to 120 degrees. That makes it as much a handheld as a pole tool, so you can cut low hedges and extend for tall ones without owning two machines.

The blade is cut to 5/8 inch and the listing mentions a double lock safety switch that needs both controls engaged before the blade moves. Two 4Ah batteries come in the kit, which gives it plenty of runtime. The long 22.4 inch blade, however, makes it the least comfortable to hold at the end of a pole.

The five positions across 120 degrees are fewer than the 11 positions offered by other 2-in-1 trimmers. It suits a yard with both low and tall hedges, where the pole is used only for the top. Check the pole joint before each use, wipe the blades after cutting and store the packs indoors. Because it doubles as a handheld, you can trim the lower two thirds of a tall hedge without the pole and add it only for the top. That habit lowers fatigue and extends the time the blades stay sharp.
products.bestFor: Yards with both low borders and a few tall hedges.
pros: Works as a handheld and a pole tool
Five head positions over 0 to 120 degrees
cons: 22.4 inch blade is heavy on a pole
Fewer head stops than some rivals

buyingCriteria.explanation: The pole length is the figure to trust. The Alloyman is listed to 8 feet, the 18 inch light kit to 8.6 feet and the YDlawn to 8 feet. The 15 and 11 feet claims on other models include the user's own height.

Add roughly 3 to 4 feet to the pole length for a person of average height with arms raised. That puts the Alloyman near 11 to 12 feet and the YDlawn near 12 to 13 feet. Measure your tallest hedge before you buy.
A long, single telescopic shaft flexes under load. Flex lowers control and makes the blade skip. Keep the head angle near 30 to 45 degrees and extend only as far as you need.
A 22 inch blade like the YDlawn covers more per pass but loads the tip with leverage. A 16 inch blade like the Alloyman is easier to hold at height. For long reach, shorter is usually safer.

The Alloyman is 8 pounds, the light kit 6 pounds and the Xssive 3 kg with a strap. The strap spreads load to your torso. If you work above shoulder height for more than ten minutes, support matters more than raw weight.

Holding a pole up uses more time than a handheld, so runtime matters. The Alloyman, YDlawn and MZK use 4.0Ah packs, the light kit 2000mAh and the Xssive one 2.0Ah. Pick two large packs for long hedges.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach honesty
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared pole length with the claimed reach. The Alloyman states pole length plainly while the YDlawn's 15 ft includes your own height.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control at height
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered blade length, weight and strap support. Shorter blades and the Xssive strap scored well.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutting fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared listed capacity. The Alloyman and Craftsman at 3/4 inch led.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery depth

cards.label: Wide blade
cards.text: The YDlawn 22 inch and MZK 22.4 inch cover more per pass. They add leverage at the tip, so they tire you faster at height.

cards.label: Short blade
cards.text: The Alloyman 16 inch and light 18 inch kit hold steadier at height. They need more passes on a long top.

howToChoose.note: Pick short for control and wide only for flat, soft hedge tops.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for pole length you can verify, a stiff shaft and a head that locks. Subtract your own height from any headline reach to find the pole's true length.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Alloyman 16 in. gives 8 ft of verified pole and 4.0Ah packs, and the YDlawn gives the most real reach. The first is steadier and the second reaches higher.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if your hedges are above 10 feet or you cut every season. The Alloyman and YDlawn kits provide large packs and honest reach.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if your hedge is just above head height. The 6 lb 18 inch kit or the Xssive does it for less.

maintenance.why: A slipping clamp drops the head. Tighten and test at full extension.
Grit makes the shaft stiff and scratches the tubes. Wipe the sections and add a drop of dry lubricant.
Sap thickens on the teeth and cuts capacity. Oil protects the steel.
Clips carry the load on strapped models. Replace worn parts.
Cold lowers capacity. Keep packs at half charge.

faq.q: How long is the real reach?
faq.a: Add roughly 3 to 4 feet to the pole length. An 8 foot pole gives about 11 to 12 feet of working height for an average person.
Only if you count your own height with arms raised. The YDlawn pole is 8 feet, so its real standing reach is closer to 12 or 13 feet.

faq.q: Why does the tool feel heavy?
faq.a: The pole acts as a lever, so weight at the head feels much greater than the number on the box. A strap and a shorter blade reduce it.

faq.q: How big a battery do I need?
faq.a: For long hedges, two 4.0Ah packs. A single 2.0Ah pack runs out quickly when you hold the tool up.
Only to the listed capacity, 5/8 to 3/4 inch. Thicker stems need a pole saw.
No. Stay well clear of overhead lines. A long pole can conduct electricity, and an unexpected touch is dangerous.
